title: Given n pairs of parentheses, generate all combinations of well-formed (balanced) parentheses.
shortTitle: Generate Parentheses — track open and close counts

s1_definition.profdef: Backtrack building the string character by character, maintaining counts of open and close parentheses used. Append an open parenthesis while open < n, and append a close parenthesis while close < open; record the string when its length reaches 2n. These two invariants guarantee only valid sequences are ever built, so no validity check is needed at the end.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of opening and closing nested approval brackets in National Bank of India's workflow. You may open a new bracket as long as you have brackets left to open, and you may only close one if there is an open bracket waiting. Follow those two rules and every sequence you build is automatically balanced.
s1_definition.oneliner: Open while open < n, close while close < open, record at length 2n — never generate an invalid string.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Backtrack building the string character by character, maintaining counts of open and close parentheses used. Append an open parenthesis while open < n, and append a close parenthesis while close < open; record the string when its length reaches 2n. These two invariants guarantee only valid sequences are ever built, so no validity check is needed at the end.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of opening and closing nested approval brackets in National Bank of India's workflow. You may open a new bracket as long as you have brackets left to open, and you may only close one if there is an open bracket waiting. Follow those two rules and every sequence you build is automatically balanced.

**One line to remember:** Open while open < n, close while close < open, record at length 2n — never generate an invalid string.

sections.s2_technical:
Carry open and close counts and a StringBuilder. When length is 2n, record the result. Otherwise, if open < n, append '(' and recurse with open+1; if close < open, append ')' and recurse with close+1; undo each append. For example: `if (open < n) { sb.append('('); backtrack(open+1, close); sb.deleteCharAt(last); }`.

The invariant `close < open` is what forbids closing more than has been opened, keeping every prefix valid. Because invalid prefixes are never created, the algorithm visits only the Catalan-number many valid strings.

The count of results is the n-th Catalan number, and the time is proportional to that count times the string length. A senior nuance is that this "build only valid states" approach is far more efficient than generating all 2^(2n) strings and filtering, which is a common naive mistake.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At National Bank of India, an approval-rule builder composes nested approval brackets, and the tool must enumerate every well-formed nesting of n bracket pairs for a template picker. This is exactly how Generate Parentheses works.

Problem 2 — A bracket can only be closed if one is currently open, and all brackets must eventually close. This is exactly why the open-and-close count invariants guarantee balanced output.

The mini-project builds an `ApprovalBracketGenerator`, a `BankLogFormatter`, and a runnable demo.

sections.s5_journey:
The input n is three.

Step 1: The recursion opens brackets while open is below three, building prefixes like ( then (( then (((.

Step 2: From (((, closes are added until balanced, yielding ((())).

Step 3: Backtracking explores other interleavings such as (()()) and (())() and ()(()) and ()()().

Step 4: Each recorded string has length six and is perfectly balanced, five in total (the third Catalan number).

sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  backtrack(open,close), len target = 2n=6
    open<n → append '('   (open++)
    close<open → append ')' (close++)
    len==6 → record
  valid-only states → Catalan(3) = 5 results
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Generate Parentheses is a backtracking problem where the elegance comes from never building an invalid string in the first place. I track two counts, how many open parentheses and how many close parentheses I have placed, and I build the string character by character. I may append an open parenthesis as long as the open count is below n, and I may append a close parenthesis only when the close count is strictly less than the open count. When the string reaches length two n it is guaranteed balanced, so I record it with no further validation.

The invariant that close must stay below open is what forbids closing a bracket that was never opened, keeping every prefix valid. Because I only ever visit valid states, I generate exactly the n-th Catalan number of strings, which is dramatically better than producing all two-to-the-two-n strings and filtering.

In my project at National Bank of India, an approval-rule builder let designers compose nested approval brackets, and the tool enumerated every well-formed nesting of n pairs for a template picker. This count-invariant backtracking produced only balanced templates, which is both faster and simpler than generate-then-filter.
